APIScope.description: APIScope is one thing a token for an API may allow — "orders:read" — which the API checks for.

is_default.description: `is_default` adds the scope to every access token for the API, whether or not it was asked for — still only when the application is allowed it and, if the API enforces roles, the user's roles grant it.

AccessAPI.description: accessAPI is what an application may do with one API.

AccessResponse.description: accessResponse is every API, with what the application may do with each.

AccessScope.description: accessScope is one scope of an API, and whether the application may ask for it.

ActorCount.description: ActorCount is how much one administrator did.

AdminPermission.description:
AdminPermission is one thing an administrator may do in the panel.

The catalog lives in code rather than in a table: each permission is a route the server guards and a control the panel shows, so a permission nothing checks for would mean nothing. Roles store the names they grant, and a name that falls out of the catalog simply stops granting anything.

scopable.description: `scopable` says the permission can be granted for one application: a role assigned to an administrator for "shop" grants its scopable permissions for shop only, and its other permissions not at all.

AdminRequest.description:
adminRequest is the body of the create and update endpoints.

There is no username: the address is the account, as it is for the first administrator. Assignments replace every role the administrator held.

email.description: An email address, at most 255 characters.

password.description: `password` is required when creating an administrator. When updating one it is optional: left empty, the password they have is kept. At most 72 characters.

status.description: `status` says whether the account may sign in. Only an active one may.

AdminResponse.description: adminResponse is the account that was just made, as the panel sees it.

AdminrolesListResponse.description: listResponse is every admin role matching a search.

AdminrolesRoleRequest.description: roleRequest is the body of the create and update endpoints. Permissions are names from the catalog, and replace what the role granted.

AdminrolesRoleResponse.description: roleResponse is one admin role as the panel sees it.

admin_count.description: `admin_count` is how many administrators hold the role.

is_builtin.description: `is_builtin` marks super_admin, which cannot be changed or removed.

permissions.description: `permissions` are the catalog names the role grants. super_admin lists every one, which is what it means.

AdminsAdminResponse.description: adminResponse is an administrator as the panel sees it. It is built by hand so the password hash and the lockout counters are never published.

mfa_enabled.description: `mfa_enabled` says whether they sign in with a second factor.

permissions.description: `permissions` are what the whole-panel roles add up to, `scoped_permissions` what the scoped ones add for each application, and `is_super_admin` whether one of the whole-panel roles is super_admin.

AdminsPageResponse.description: pageResponse is a page of administrators.

ApiRequest.description: apiRequest is the body of the create and update endpoints. The scopes replace the API's: a scope sent with its id is kept, with every allowance and grant of it; one sent without is new; one left out is removed.

enforce_roles.description: `enforce_roles` and `allow_offline_access` may be left out: a new API then enforces roles and refuses refresh tokens; an existing one keeps them.

signing_algorithm.description: `signing_algorithm` left empty is RS256. `token_lifetime` is in seconds, and zero leaves it to each application.

ApiResponse.description: apiResponse is an API as the panel sees it.

application_count.description: `application_count` is how many applications may ask for tokens for it, and `role_count` how many roles grant at least one of its scopes.

issuer.description: `issuer` and `jwks_uri` are what an API validating its tokens needs from this server: the iss to expect, and where the signing keys are.

system.description: `system` is "admin" or "account" for an API this server is itself, whose identifier and scopes the panel shows but does not change.

ApisListResponse.description: listResponse is every API matching a search.

AppRef.description: appRef names an application a role belongs to.

ApplicationRequest.description:
applicationRequest is the body of the create and update endpoints. The names are RFC 7591's client metadata where it has one.

Type is read on create only: it decides whether the app is a public client, which cannot change once copies of it are in use. A lifetime left at zero takes the default.

allow_registration.description: `allow_registration` may be left out too: a new application then offers registration on its sign-in page.

assert_roles.description: The flags may be left out: a new application is then enabled, requires PKCE and puts roles in its tokens; an existing one keeps its settings.

login_flow_id.description: `login_flow_id` is the flow this application signs people in with. An empty string puts it back on the default flow; leaving it out leaves the flow it has.

ApplicationResponse.description: applicationResponse is an application as the panel sees it. The secret's hash is never part of it.

login_flow_id.description: `login_flow_id` is the flow this application signs people in with, null for the default one. The panel has the flows themselves; what belongs here is which of them this application named.

role_count.description: `role_count` is how many roles the application defines.

ApplicationRoles.description: applicationRoles is what a user holds in one application.

effective_roles.description: `effective_roles` are those plus every role of the scope they include, sorted by name. This is the list a token carries.

roles.description: `roles` are the roles given to the user directly.

ApplicationsPageResponse.description: pageResponse is a page of applications.

AssignRequest.description: assignRequest is the body of the endpoint that gives a user roles: the ids of the roles to add, global and application roles alike.

AssignmentRequest.description: assignmentRequest gives the administrator one role, for the whole panel when ApplicationID is null or for that one application.

AssignmentResponse.description: assignmentResponse is one role an administrator holds, and where.

application.description: `application` is the application the role is held for, or null for the whole panel.

AuthAdminResponse.description: adminResponse is an administrator as the browser sees it. It is built by hand rather than returning the model, so a column added later cannot accidentally start being published.

mfa_enabled.description: `mfa_enabled` says whether they sign in with a second factor.

permissions.description: `permissions` are what those roles allow, `scoped_permissions` what roles held for one application add there, and `is_super_admin` whether they may manage administrators. The panel shows and hides its controls by these; the server checks them regardless.

roles.description: `roles` are the names of the roles held for the whole panel.

AuthorizeRequest.description: authorizeRequest is the body of the endpoint that authorises an application for an API: the ids of the API's scopes it may ask for.

CachingOverviewResponse.description: overviewResponse is both databases, or neither when there is no Redis.

CodeRequest.description: codeRequest is a code from an authenticator app, or a recovery code.

ConnectionRequest.description:
connectionRequest is what a create or an update sends.

Every field is a pointer because an update is a PATCH: nil is "not sent", and the stored value stands. The slug and the protocol are read only when a connection is made — both are in the addresses its provider was given. The client secret is never sent back, so an update without one keeps the one there is.

name.description: Omitnil, at least 1 characters, at most 100 characters.

ConnectionResponse.description: connectionResponse is a connection as the panel shows it: what is stored, never the secrets; how many people sign in through it; what to give the identity provider; and, for SAML, what its metadata says.

create_users.description: `create_users` makes an account for someone signing in for the first time.

domains.description: `domains` are the email domains the connection signs people in for, lower case. A domain belongs to one connection at most. None is every address, and then the button on the sign-in page is the only way to the connection, since no address leads to it.

email_attribute.description: The names of the claims or attributes to read. Empty is the protocol's usual ones (SSOAttributeDefaults).

enforce_domains.description: `enforce_domains` makes the connection the only way in for its domains.

issuer.description: OpenID Connect: the issuer, whose discovery document says everything else, and the client this server is registered as there.

matching.description: `matching` is what to do with an address this server already has.

metadata_url.description: SAML 2.0: the provider's metadata — fetched from `metadata_url`, or pasted in when the provider only offers a file — which carries its entity ID, its sign-in address and the certificate its assertions are signed with.

name.description: `name` is what the sign-in page calls it: "Continue with <name>".

name_id_format.description: `name_id_format` is what to ask the provider to identify people by.

role_mappings.description: `role_mappings` give a role to everybody the provider puts in a group.

show_on_login.description: `show_on_login` puts a button for the connection on the sign-in page. Off, people reach it by typing an address at one of its domains.

sign_requests.description: `sign_requests` signs the authentication requests sent to the provider, for the providers that require it.

slug.description: `slug` names the connection in the addresses the provider is given — /oauth2/sso/<slug>/callback, /acs, /metadata — so it cannot change once the provider has them.

sync_profile.description: `sync_profile` rewrites the user's name from the provider on every sign-in: the provider is where it is kept.

sync_roles.description: `sync_roles` also takes a mapped role away from someone no longer in its group. Off, mapped roles are only ever added.

ContentRequest.description: contentRequest is one language's words for the emails: the keys of model.MailMessageSpecs and what they say. A key with an empty value clears the override rather than storing a blank, and the shipped text comes back.

ContentResponse.description: contentResponse is every email the server sends and every language it can be sent in: the catalog once, and the text per language.

Counts.description: Counts are the numbers on the dashboard: how much of everything there is.

CreateRequest.description:
createRequest is what adding a language sends.

CopyFrom names where its text starts: another language here, whose text is copied — Portuguese for Brazilian Portuguese — or a language the server ships with that this installation has not got, which brings its shipped text back. Empty is a language with nothing translated yet, whose pages show the base language's text until somebody writes its own.

editable.description: `editable` says whether its cached values may be replaced by hand: the cache database's may, the session database's never.

DayCount.description: DayCount is one day of the activity chart.

day.description: `day` is the date in the database's time zone, as YYYY-MM-DD.

failures.description: `failures` are the sign-ins refused that day, wrong passwords and blocked accounts together.

Enrolment.description: Enrolment is an authenticator being set up: what the app needs.

EventResponse.description: eventResponse is one entry of the activity list.

FieldRequest.description: fieldRequest is what a create sends: the same rules, plus what the field is.

FieldResponse.description:
fieldResponse is one field as the panel sees it.

It is built by hand rather than returning the model because the two kinds of field are not the same shape: an additional one is a row and has an id and timestamps, while a built-in one is a column of the record and has none. Sending a row's fields for something that is not a row would be saying it has an id of all zeros, which is not true.

FlowRequest.description:
flowRequest is what a create or an update sends.

Every field is a pointer because an update is a PATCH: nil is "not sent", and the stored value stands. A create reads the same struct — what it leaves out is taken from the flow a new installation starts with, so the panel can save a flow that is a name and nothing else.

FlowResponse.description: flowResponse is a flow as the panel sees it: the record, plus the two things the panel would otherwise have to work out for itself — how many applications hold it, and whether every step it names is one this server runs yet.

applications.description: `applications` is how many applications name this flow. The ones that name none are not counted: they follow whichever flow is the default.

planned.description: `planned` are the steps this flow names that the sign-in pages do not run yet. Empty means the flow is the sign-in it describes.

FlowsListResponse.description: listResponse is what the list endpoint answers with: the flows, and the catalog the panel builds its step picker from.

FlowsResponse.description: response is what the single-flow endpoints answer with.

known.description: `known` says the server reads the group; one it does not is holding values from before, left to expire.

HeldRoles.description: heldRoles is what a user holds in one scope.

effective_roles.description: `effective_roles` are those plus every role of the scope they include, sorted by name. This is the list a token carries.

roles.description: `roles` are the roles given to the user directly.

IdentityProvider.description: identityProvider is what a SAML provider's metadata says about it, so the panel can show it is the right one — and when its certificate runs out, which is the usual way a working connection stops working.

KeyInfo.description: KeyInfo describes one signing key, for administrators.

ttl_seconds.description: `ttl_seconds` is how long it has left, or -1 for a key that does not expire.

KeysResponse.description: keysResponse is a page of keys and where the next one starts: an empty cursor after the last page.

LanguageContent.description: languageContent is one language's words for the emails: what it says, and what English says, key by key.

base.description: `base` is the shipped English for the same keys, which is what an email goes out in where a language has nothing.

messages.description: `messages` is what this language says, for the email keys alone, and only where it says something: a key it is missing falls back to `base`.

offered.description: `offered` is whether the sign-in pages are shown in this language. One that is not still has its text, and the panel marks it.

LanguageRequest.description:
languageRequest is what an update sends.

Every field is a pointer because this is a PATCH: nil is "not sent", and the stored value stands. The code is not among them — it is in the path, and it is what every reader's saved choice names.

name.description: Omitnil, at least 1 characters, at most 64 characters.

native_name.description: Omitnil, at least 1 characters, at most 64 characters.

LanguageResponse.description: languageResponse is one language as the panel sees it: its settings, and how much of each app it translates.

apps.description: `apps` are the apps this language is translated for, which today is the sign-in pages and nothing else.

base.description: `base` marks the language every other is a translation of: it cannot be turned off or removed.

coverage.description: `coverage` is how much of each of those apps is translated, as a percentage of the keys the base language has, and `missing` how many keys each is short. The keys are the app names.

name.description: `name` is what the language is called in English, Native what it calls itself.

shipped.description: `shipped` says the server ships a translation of this language, so a key a release adds reaches it on the next start.

LanguagesListResponse.description: listResponse is what the list endpoint answers with.

apps.description: `apps` are the two catalogs a language is counted against, so the panel names the columns from the server rather than from a list of its own.

LanguagesResponse.description: response is what the single-language endpoints answer with.

Limits.description: limits are the bounds the panel holds its fields to, from the model, so the two cannot disagree about what a code may be.

ListRequest.description: listRequest is the Sessions page's query string: an address to search by its start, one user's sessions, and the session to continue after.

ListResponse.description:
listResponse is every field a user record has, and the types a new one may have. Both come together because the panel's form needs the second to offer the first.

The built-in fields come first and are marked as such: the panel draws its table and its form from this one list, and uses the mark to know which of them it may offer to change.

LogResponse.description: logResponse is the same entry on the logs page, which has room for more.

LoginRequest.description:
loginRequest is the body of POST /admin/auth/login.

The password has no rule beyond being there: what a password must look like is the account's business, and a sign-in form that explains the policy is a sign-in form that helps someone guessing.

LoginStepSpec.description: LoginStepSpec describes one step for the panel: what it is called, what it does, and whether this server runs it yet.

fixed.description: `fixed` steps cannot be removed or moved: a flow that does not ask who is signing in has nobody to sign in.

implemented.description: `implemented` says the sign-in pages run this step today. A flow may name one that is not, and the panel marks it: the flow is a plan the server is being built towards, not a promise it already keeps.

MFAStatus.description: MFAStatus is what an administrator sees about their own second factor.

MailMessageSpec.description:
MailMessageSpec is one email this server sends, for the panel to list: what it is called, when it goes out, and the keys its subject and body are written under.

The text itself is not here. It is the sign-in pages' text, in the languages table, so a message goes out in the reader's language and is translated by whoever translates the rest — the Mail page edits those keys rather than holding a second copy of them.

params.description: `params` are the {braces} the text may use, each with what it stands for, so the panel can list them beside the editor and refuse one it does not know.

subject_key.description: `subject_key` and `body_key` are the keys in the sign-in pages' catalog.

MailParam.description: MailParam is one placeholder a message's text may use.

MailResponse.description: response is what the two settings endpoints answer with. The encryptions come along so the panel builds its picker from the server's catalog rather than from a list of its own.

MailTestRequest.description: testRequest is a test message: where to send it, and the settings to send it with. The settings are the form's, so a server can be tried before it is saved; what the form leaves out is the stored value.

MappedRole.description: mappedRole is one role a user holds, as the role mapping tab lists it.

application.description: `application` is the application the role belongs to, or null for a global role.

assigned.description: `assigned` says the role was given to the user directly, and `via` lists the directly given roles it also comes through. A role with `via` and not `assigned` is inherited; one with both is given directly and also implied, and taking it away leaves the user holding it.

composite.description: `composite` says the role includes other roles.

MappingsResponse.description: mappingsResponse is every role a user holds: global roles first, then each application's, each sorted by name.

MfaCodeRequest.description: codeRequest is a code from the authenticator app, or a recovery code.

OptionalCodeRequest.description: optionalCodeRequest is the body of starting a set-up: a code from the current authenticator when one is being replaced, and nothing otherwise.

OrganizationBrand.description: organizationBrand is the part of the organisation the panel's header shows: what it is called, and its logo. Only what the sign-in pages already publish to anyone belongs in it.

OrganizationRequest.description:
organizationRequest is what an update sends.

Every field is a pointer because this is a PATCH: nil is "not sent", and the stored value stands. An empty string is sent on purpose and clears the setting — which only the ones that may be empty accept.

OrganizationResponse.description: organizationResponse is the organisation as the panel sees it. It is built by hand rather than returning the model so the row's own bookkeeping — its id, when it was last written — stays out of a record of settings, and the one date worth showing is named for what it means.

OtpResponse.description: response is what both endpoints answer with.

OtpSettingsRequest.description:
settingsRequest is what an update sends.

Every field is a pointer because this is a PATCH: nil is "not sent", and the stored value stands.

OtpSettingsResponse.description: settingsResponse is the settings as the panel sees them, built by hand so the row's own bookkeeping stays out of a record of settings.

days.description: `days` is the range everything below was counted over.

PageResponse.description: pageResponse is a page of users, with enough about the page for the panel to say "1 of 4" without asking again.

PasswordRequest.description: passwordRequest is the body of POST /admin/me/password.

PreviewRequest.description: previewRequest is a token request to evaluate: who for (nil for the application itself), which API, and the scope parameter as an application would send it.

Problem.description: An error the API answers with. `code` is stable, and what an application should act on; `error` is its English sentence; `params` fills in the sentence's {placeholders}.

ProfileRequest.description: profileRequest is the body of PATCH /admin/me: the administrator's own name and address. The current password is only needed when the address changes, since the address is what they sign in with.

email.description: An email address, at most 255 characters.

ProviderRequest.description:
providerRequest is what a create or an update sends.

Every settable field is a pointer, because this is a PATCH: a request that does not mention a setting leaves it as it is, the way the organisation's endpoint works. It matters more here than anywhere else — a caller turning a provider off sends `{"enabled": false}`, and that must not quietly empty the endpoints and keys around it.

The secrets are pointers for a second reason: they cannot be sent back, so only a request carrying a new value replaces one.

kind.description: `kind` and `slug` are read when a provider is registered and never again: the slug is in the address registered with the provider, and the kind decides which addresses those are.

position.description: `position` is where the button sits. Left out, a new provider goes last and an existing one stays where it is.

token_auth.description: `token_auth` is how the secret is presented at the token endpoint. An empty string leaves it to the kind's own default.

ProviderResponse.description:
providerResponse is a configured provider as the panel sees it.

The secrets are not in it, and never are: a secret that has been stored can be replaced but not read back, so the panel is told only whether there is one. The callback address is here because it is what an administrator has to paste into the provider's console, and only this server knows it.

callback_url.description: `callback_url` is what the provider has to be told to send people back to.

identities.description: `identities` is how many users sign in with this provider.

token_auth.description: `token_auth` is what the record says, which may be empty; `token_auth_used` is what that comes to, the kind's own default included.

Reference.description: reference names another row: enough to show it and to send it back.

Response.description: response is what both endpoints answer with.

RoleMapping.description: roleMapping is one group given one role.

RoleRequest.description:
roleRequest is the body of the create and update endpoints.

Inherits holds ids, and replaces what the role had: an update sends the whole role, the same as for a user.

api_scopes.description: `api_scopes` are the ids of the API scopes the role grants, and replace what it granted. Left out, the role keeps its grants — so an administrator who cannot see APIs can still edit the rest of it.

application_id.description: `application_id` is the application the role belongs to, or null for a global role. It is read on create only: a role keeps its scope.

is_default.description: `is_default` gives the role to every user created without roles of their own.

RoleResponse.description: roleResponse is one role as the panel sees it.

api_scopes.description: `api_scopes` are the API scopes the role grants directly.

application_id.description: `application_id` is the application the role belongs to, or null for a global role.

inherited_roles.description: `inherited_roles` is every role holding this one includes once inheritance is followed all the way down, sorted by name. Roles of applications the administrator cannot see are left out.

inherits.description: `inherits` are the roles this one includes directly.

user_count.description: `user_count` is how many users hold the role directly.

RolesPageResponse.description: pageResponse is a page of roles, with enough about the page for the panel to say how many there are without asking again.

RolesResponse.description: rolesResponse is the roles a user holds as tokens would carry them: the global roles, and each application's. An application the user holds nothing in is still listed, with empty lists.

RolesRoleRef.description: roleRef names another role, and its scope: enough to show it and to send it back.

RotateRequest.description: rotateRequest is the body of POST /admin/signing-keys/rotate. Both may be left out, for a scheduled rotation that follows the usual lead.

immediate.description: `immediate` makes the new keys sign now, and retires the old ones.

revoke_old.description: `revoke_old` deletes the old keys as well, so APIs stop trusting every token they signed. It implies `immediate`.

RulesRequest.description: rulesRequest is what an update sends: what a field expects of its values. Its name and its type are not here, because neither may change once records hold values under them.

SSORoleMapping.description: SSORoleMapping gives a role to the members of one group at the provider.

SavedResponse.description: savedResponse is what saving a translation answers with: the language as it now counts, and how many keys of what was sent were not ones the app looks up — a file from an older release, or a typo.

ScopeDecision.description: ScopeDecision is what happened to one requested scope, and why.

is_default.description: `is_default` marks an API scope that was not asked for, but added because the API makes it a default.

ScopeRef.description: scopeRef names an API scope, and the API it belongs to.

ScopeRequest.description: scopeRequest is one scope of an API.

ScopeResponse.description: scopeResponse is one scope of an API.

SecretResponse.description: secretResponse is an application together with a client secret that was just made. The secret is only ever in this one answer; it is left out when none was made.

SecurityRequest.description: securityRequest is what a change to the settings that apply to every administrator sends. The flag is a pointer so a request that does not mention it leaves it alone.

SecurityResponse.description: securityResponse is how administrators are made to sign in, and what that means for the ones there are: the panel says how many would be asked to set an authenticator up before it turns the requirement on.

administrators.description: `administrators` is how many there are, and `with_mfa` how many of those already sign in with a second factor.

ServiceProvider.description: serviceProvider is what the identity provider is set up with: for OpenID Connect the redirect URI, for SAML the assertion consumer service, the entity ID, the metadata that says both, and the certificate requests are signed with.

SessionResponse.description: sessionResponse is one of the places an administrator is signed in.

current.description: `current` is the session this request came from: the browser reading the list, which is signed out rather than ended from it.

SessionsListResponse.description: listResponse is a page of sessions, and the session to continue after when there are more — never a total, which would mean counting every session there is on every visit.

SessionsSessionResponse.description: sessionResponse is one session as the panel lists it.

SettingsRequest.description:
settingsRequest is what an update sends.

Every field is a pointer because this is a PATCH: nil is "not sent", and the stored value stands. That matters most for the password — the panel never has the stored one to send back, so leaving it out is how a form saves without changing it, and an empty string is how it is cleared.

SettingsResponse.description: settingsResponse is the mail settings as the panel sees them. It is built by hand rather than returning the model so the row's own bookkeeping stays out of a record of settings — and so the password cannot leave by accident: what is said about it is whether there is one.

has_password.description: `has_password` says a password is stored, without saying what it is. The form shows "set" rather than asking for one that is already there.

SetupRequest.description:
setupRequest is the form the first administrator is made from.

There is no username: the address is the account. Asking for one more thing to remember, at the one moment someone is trying to get in for the first time, buys nothing.

email.description: An email address, at most 255 characters.

password.description: At least 10 characters, at most 128 characters.

ShippedResponse.description: shippedResponse is a language the server ships with that this installation does not have — one somebody removed, or one that shipped after it started — which the panel offers to add back.

SignIns.description: SignIns is how signing in to the panel has gone since a moment.

SocialAccount.description: SocialAccount is one provider a user signs in with, as their record shows it: enough to say which account at the provider it is, and to disconnect it.

id.description: `id` is the identity's, which is what disconnecting it names.

SocialListResponse.description: listResponse is every provider, and the kinds one may be. Both come together because the panel's form needs the second to offer the first: what a kind's endpoints are, whether it asks for them, and where to register this server with it.

SocialSpec.description: SocialSpec is everything about a kind that is the same in every installation: where to send people, what to ask for, and how to read the answer. The catalog is in code rather than in a table for the same reason the admin permissions are — a provider that moves an endpoint is a change to this file, not to everybody's database.

authorize_url.description: The endpoints. Empty in a kind whose provider is not known in advance, where the record carries them instead.

custom.description: `custom` says the endpoints come from the record, and the panel asks for them.

docs.description: `docs` is where an administrator registers this server with the provider.

label.description: `label` is what the panel calls it, and the name a new provider is given.

scopes.description: `scopes` is what to ask for unless the record says otherwise.

signed_secret.description: `signed_secret` says the client secret is a JWT this server signs with a registered key, rather than a secret the provider gave out (Apple).

token_auth.description: `token_auth` is how this kind's provider wants the secret presented. A record of a custom kind may say otherwise.

StatusResponse.description: statusResponse says whether the panel still needs an administrator.

TargetResponse.description: targetResponse is what an entry happened to. Name is left out when the record is gone or the administrator may not see what it is called.

TestRequest.description: testRequest is a connection's provider to try before saving: an issuer to discover, or metadata to read.

scopes.description: At most 32 items, at most 128 items.

TestResponse.description: testResponse is what trying a provider found.

identity_provider.description: For SAML, what its metadata said, and the metadata itself when it was fetched, so the panel can keep it.

issuer.description: For OpenID Connect, the endpoints its discovery document gave.

unsupported_scopes.description: `unsupported_scopes` are the scopes the connection would ask for that the provider does not list. Some providers refuse the whole sign-in over one — Keycloak answers invalid_scope — so the panel warns before anybody tries.

TokenPreview.description: TokenPreview is what a token request amounts to: whether a token is issued at all, the decision on every scope, and the claims each token carries.

access_token_header.description: `access_token_header` is the JOSE header of the access token: how it is signed, and that it is a JWT access token (RFC 9068).

TranslationRequest.description:
translationRequest is one language's whole text for one app, replacing what was there: what the editor saves, and what an imported file is.

`$name` and `$native` may come along — a file a translator wrote carries them — and are ignored here: the names are the language's own settings.

TranslationResponse.description: translationResponse is one language's text for one app, as the editor needs it: the keys there are, the base language's text beside each, and what this language has.

base.description: `base` is the text the base language shows, every key filled in: what the translator is translating, and what a missing key falls back to.

has_password.description: `has_password` tells the panel whether a password is set, without telling it anything about the password.

is_password_temporary.description: `is_password_temporary` marks a password an administrator chose for the user, which the user is expected to replace the next time they sign in.

last_login_at.description: `last_login_at` is when the user last signed in to an application.

roles.description: `roles` are the roles given to this user directly. What they add up to, inheritance included, is RoleGraph.Effective.

social_accounts.description: `social_accounts` are the providers this user signs in with. Like `has_password` it is no column: the panel is told what a record amounts to, and the rows themselves are social_identities.

UserRequest.description:
userRequest is the body of the create and update endpoints.

The named fields are the built-in ones: they are columns of the record, so they are spelled out here and held to the rules in the tags. Data carries the additional fields an organisation added, whose rules live in user_fields and are applied in validation.go.

email.description: An email address, at most 255 characters.

is_email_verified.description: `is_email_verified` and `is_active` may be left out: a new user is then unverified and active, and an existing one keeps what they had.

is_password_temporary.description: `is_password_temporary` marks the password as one the user has to replace. Left out, a new user's password is not temporary and an existing user's keeps what it was.

password.description: `password` is required when creating a user. When updating one it is optional: left empty, the password the user has is kept. At most 72 characters.

UserRole.description:
UserRole is a role users hold, either across every application or in one.

A global role belongs to no application — Keycloak's realm roles — and is the same role wherever the user signs in: "employee", "beta-tester". An application role belongs to the application that defines it — Keycloak's client roles, Zitadel's project roles, Entra's app roles — so "admin" in one app says nothing about another. A name is unique within its scope: once among the global roles, and once within each application.

This server says which roles a user holds; what a role lets them do is decided by the applications, so a role carries no permissions of its own.

A role can be composite, inheriting other roles: holding "editor" also means holding "viewer". As in Keycloak, a global role may include global roles and any application's roles, and an application role may include global roles and roles of its own application. A role marked default is given to every user created.

api_scopes.description: `api_scopes` are the API scopes holding this role grants. A token for an API carries one only when the application is allowed it too.

application_id.description: `application_id` is the application the role belongs to, or nil for a global role.

UsingFlow.description: usingFlow is one login flow that asks for an emailed code, so the page can say who these settings are for rather than leaving an administrator to guess whether anything reads them.

ValueResponse.description: valueResponse is a key with what it holds.

ttl_seconds.description: `ttl_seconds` is how long it has left, or -1 for a key that does not expire.

WriteRequest.description: writeRequest is the body of the endpoint that replaces a cached value.

ttl_seconds.description: `ttl_seconds` is how long it should live; left out or zero keeps what it had left.

value.description: `value` is the new value, as JSON of any shape.
